newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: CBA'S MURRAY HAPPY WITH LONG TERM OUTLOOK.
newsitem.headline: CBA'S MURRAY HAPPY WITH LONG TERM OUTLOOK.

text.p: The managing director of Commonwealth Bank of Australia (CBA), David Murray, said on Thursday he was optimistic about the bank's long term earnings outlook.

Speaking to reporters after a luncheon address, Murray said the bank would have a testing year and many others banks would also be challenged as the whole industry adjusted to thinner margins in the home lending market.
Asked if he was optimistic for the bank's earnings outlook Murray said: "I'm optimistic about the long term future of my plan. I've got to be."
Murray said the bank was still making a lot of investments for its build-up in financial services distribution and regarded those investments as long term.
"On the other hand, we are making some productivity improvements and we are increasing our income outside our normal business," Murray said.

Murray said CBA's decision to lead the major banks in a home loan market price war against non-banks funded by securitisation was a difficult one but one which put the bank in a good position for the long term.

Asked about further cost reductions, Murray said changes in the finacial services distribution system would lead to fewer jobs in that area but more people would be needed in direct banking and other financial services.
"This will probably mean less agregate employment but more interesting work for those in employment," he said.
Murray said the bank would like to lower its cost to income ratio below the 60 percent level compared to the 61.1 percent level for 1996/97 year.
But Murray said it was dangerous to place too much emphasis on the cost to income ratio because it did not include write-offs of goodwill.

"If I were to buy a whole series of banks and get efficiency gains from that and improve the top line, I would have a rapidly improving cost to income ratio but it may not be the best long term outcome for shareholders to buy a stack of banks," he said.
Murray said Canadian banks were very efficient for their community with very thin lending margins but shareholder returns averaging 16 percent but a cost to income ratio of 61 percent to 62 percent.
"You can't judge a cost to income ratio in isolation and you can't judge it without looking at the circumstances and the build-up of the business," Murray said.
